question: Which WirelessHART data-link mechanism provides reliable, collision-free, and deterministic communication?

options.text: Superframes divided into 10-millisecond TDMA time slots
CSMA/CD over a wired Ethernet bus

explanation: WirelessHART data link layer divides time into fixed 10-millisecond TDMA time slots organized into recurring superframes, enabling collision-free, deterministic real-time communication for industrial wireless networks.

question: In WirelessHART, which entity supervises network nodes and guides them regarding when and where packets should be transmitted?
explanation: The Network Manager in WirelessHART is the centralized supervisory entity that manages routing tables, schedule configurations, and guides nodes on exact transmission slots.

question: Which of the following are operating modes of NFC?
explanation: NFC defines three standardized operating modes: Peer-to-peer mode (device-to-device data exchange), Read/write mode (reading/writing to passive NFC tags), and Card-emulation mode (acting as a contactless smart card).

question: Which of the following are phases of Bluetooth connection establishment?
explanation: Bluetooth connection establishment follows three sequential phases: Inquiry/discovery phase (detecting surrounding devices), Paging phase (synchronizing clock and forming piconet), and Connected phase (data transmission).

question: In which Bluetooth operating mode does a slave remain inactive until the master instructs it to wake up?
explanation: In Bluetooth Park mode, a slave gives up its active MAC address, sleeps to conserve power, and remains inactive until the master instructs it to unpark and wake up.

question: Which of the following functions are provided by the Bluetooth L2CAP layer?

options.text: Generation of the magnetic field used by NFC tags

explanation: L2CAP (Logical Link Control and Adaptation Protocol) provides protocol multiplexing, segmentation and reassembly (SAR) of large packets, and both connection-oriented and connectionless data services for higher-layer protocols.

question: A single Z-Wave network can contain up to approximately how many nodes?
explanation: Z-Wave specifies that a single network mesh can address up to 232 nodes using its 8-bit Node ID addressing scheme.

question: Which of the following statements about Z-Wave addressing are correct?

options.text: Each logical Z-Wave network has one Home ID.
A Z-Wave Node ID has a length of one byte.
A Z-Wave Home ID has a length of four bytes.
Nodes having different Home IDs can communicate directly with one another.

explanation: In Z-Wave, Home ID is a 4-byte (32-bit) unique identifier shared by all devices in the same network, while Node ID is a 1-byte (8-bit) device address. Devices with different Home IDs cannot directly communicate without an inter-network gateway.

question: Which of the following statements about ISA 100.11a are correct?

options.text: Its network and transport layers are based on TCP, UDP, or IPv6.
Its data-link layer supports mesh networking with frequency hopping.
Its radio is based on IEEE 802.15.4.
It supports only a ring topology.

explanation: ISA 100.11a uses IEEE 802.15.4 physical radio, an advanced data link layer supporting mesh routing with channel hopping, and standard IPv6/UDP/TCP network and transport protocols.

question: Why is multi-hop communication commonly used in a wireless sensor network?

options.text: Sensor nodes have short transmission ranges, so intermediate nodes relay data toward the sink.
Every sensor node must communicate directly with the Internet.
Multi-hop communication eliminates the need for a sink node.
Only mobile sensor nodes are permitted to transmit data.

explanation: Sensor nodes have low power and short radio reach; multi-hop forwarding uses intermediate peers to relay packets across wide geographic fields toward the centralized base station/sink.

question: Which of the following is described as an optional unit of a sensor node?
explanation: While power, processing, sensing, and transceiver units are mandatory baseline components of every sensor node, a location-finding system (such as GPS) or mobilizer is an application-specific optional component.

question: If n denotes the number of nodes in a sensor network, the lecture states that the throughput decreases approximately at what rate as the network scales?
explanation: According to the classic Gupta and Kumar scaling law presented in the lecture, per-node throughput in a multihop wireless sensor network scales as Θ(1/√n) due to interference and packet forwarding overhead.

question: Which types of sensor-node misbehavior are classified as intentional?
explanation: Intentional misbehavior stems from purposeful actions: malicious behavior (adversarial attacks/tampering) and selfish behavior (refusing to forward others' packets to preserve battery). Hardware faults/failures are unintentional.

question: What distinguishes a badly failed sensor node from an ordinarily failed sensor node?

options.text: It additionally sends false routing messages.
It always increases the network throughput.
It changes from a mobile node into a stationary node.
It communicates normally but consumes no power.

explanation: An ordinarily failed node simply stops operating or dropping packets, whereas a badly failed node continues broadcasting corrupt, deceptive, or false routing messages that actively mislead peers.

question: Which consequence may arise when a selfish sensor node refuses to cooperate because forwarding involves a personal cost?

options.text: It forwards every received packet twice.
It drops a received packet instead of forwarding it.
It automatically becomes the sink node.
It increases the communication range of neighboring nodes.

explanation: A selfish node seeks to conserve its limited energy battery for its own sensor readings; therefore, it silently drops packets intended for multihop routing rather than burning energy to forward them.
